scenes.title: Where and when
narration: Krishnanattam was created by Manaveda (1585–1658 AD), the Zamorin Raja of Kozhikode in northern Kerala.
Completed on 16 November 1653 when Manaveda was 68 years old, the dance drama is rooted in his Sanskrit text, Krishnagiti.

The work draws literary inspiration from the 10th and 11th skandhas of the Bhagavata Purana, Jayadeva's Gita Govinda, the Sree Krishna Vilaasam Mahakavya, and Melpathur Narayana Bhattathiri's Narayaniyam.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: The performance cycle consists of eight sequential plays: Avataram, Kaliyamardanam, Rasakrida, Kamsavadham, Swayamvaram, Banayuddham, Vividavadham, and Swargarohanam, remembered by the mnemonic "a-ka-ra-ka-swa-bha-vi-swa".
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Performed exclusively by men and young boys as a nocturnal temple act, Krishnanattam synthesizes the four dramatic aspects defined by Bharata Muni: movement (Angika), vocal text (Vachika), costume/makeup (Aharya), and emotional state (Satvika).
Performers undergo rigorous training starting around age ten for dynamic roles (vesham) and music, or age five for chutti makeup application and playing the Madhalam drum.
The movement language blends physical expression with rhythmic coordination.

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Music in Krishnanattam relies on Sanskrit slokas and padyageethams patterned after the poetic forms of Jayadeva's Gita Govinda.
The vocal text is supported by traditional percussion, prominently featuring the Madhalam drum.
Listen for the Madhalam.
Resonant vocal recitation of Sanskrit slokas accompanied by rhythmic Madhalam drumming, creating a solemn, sacred atmosphere suited for nocturnal temple ritual.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Costumes and makeup in Krishnanattam are handcrafted by the teachers and artists.
Male characters wear a starched gathered petticoat beneath a white skirt featuring horizontal orange/orange-red and black stripes near the bottom.

Their upper dress consists of a long-sleeved shirt open at the back, a wooden breast-plate, chest ornaments of beads and fresh flora, upper arm bands, wrist ornaments, a girdle, and shawls fitted with mirrors at each end.

scenes.title: The people
narration: The central historical figure of Krishnanattam is Samoothiri Manavedan Raja (1585–1658 AD), the Zamorin Raja of Kozhikode.
Educated by Anayath Krishna Pisharody and Desamangalath Varrier, Manaveda authored the Poorva Bharatha Champu in 1643 before completing Krishnagiti in 1653.
Krishnanattam is intrinsically bound to the Guruvayur Sri Krishna Temple in Thrissur district, Kerala.
Krishnanattam directly inspired and paved the way for Kathakali, another major classical dance-drama form of Kerala.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: Krishnanattam is a sacred ritual dance-drama performed near the sanctum sanctorum of the Guruvayur Sri Krishna temple as an offering by devotees. The headgear, especially Sri Krishna's peacock-feathered crown, is treated with extreme sacredness. Before applying make-up, actors prostrate before an oil lamp in devotion to Lord Guruvayoorappan.

wardrobe.from_sources: Costumes and makeup in Krishnanattam are handcrafted by the teachers and artists. Male characters wear a starched gathered petticoat beneath a white skirt featuring horizontal orange/orange-red and black stripes near the bottom. Their upper dress consists of a long-sleeved shirt open at the back, a wooden breast-plate, chest ornaments of beads and fresh flora, upper arm bands, wrist ornaments, a girdle, and shawls fitted with mirrors at each end. Female roles wear long floor-length gathered white skirts with red borders, back-tied long-sleeved blouses, wooden breast-plates covered in red cloth, and ankle bells (chilanka). Face makeup utilizes three basic colors: pazhuppu (red-dominant orange), minukku (yellow-dominant orange), and paccha (yellow-green). A chutti—two white protruding borders along the jawline—frames paccha make-up. The most sacred garment is the headgear, which comes in two primary forms: a bun (mudi) and a crown (kiriitam) topped with peacock feathers.

visual_brief.costume_notes: Costumes and makeup in Krishnanattam are handcrafted by the teachers and artists. Male characters wear a starched gathered petticoat beneath a white skirt featuring horizontal orange/orange-red and black stripes near the bottom. Their upper dress consists of a long-sleeved shirt open at the back, a wooden breast-plate, chest ornaments of beads and fresh flora, upper arm bands, wrist ornaments, a girdle, and shawls fitted with mirrors at each end. Female roles wear long floor-length gathered white skirts with red borders, back-tied long-sleeved blouses, wooden breast-plates covered in red cloth, and ankle bells (chilanka). Face makeup utilizes three basic colors: pazhuppu (red-dominant orange), minukku (yellow-dominant orange), and paccha (yellow-green). A chutti—two white protruding borders along the jawline—frames paccha make-up. The most sacred garment is the headgear, which comes in two primary forms: a bun (mudi) and a crown (kiriitam) topped with peacock feathers.
visual_brief.setting_notes: The performance cycle consists of eight sequential plays: Avataram, Kaliyamardanam, Rasakrida, Kamsavadham, Swayamvaram, Banayuddham, Vividavadham, and Swargarohanam, remembered by the mnemonic "a-ka-ra-ka-swa-bha-vi-swa". Each play is staged as a devotional offering with specific spiritual intentions: Avataram for the birth of a child, Kaliyamardanam to remove poison, Rasakrida for the well-being of unmarried girls and marital harmony, Kamsavadham to conquer enemies, Swayamvaram for happy matrimony, Banayuddham and Vividavadham to end poverty and ensure good harvests, and Swargarohanam for the peace of a departed soul. Because concluding with Lord Krishna's demise in Swargarohanam is deemed inauspicious, Avataram is traditionally repeated on a ninth night.
